Napkin
NAP-kin
noun
From the Old French nappe, “a cloth,” with the diminutive -kin; the KJV’s rendering of the Greek soudarion (a Latin loan, sudarium, “sweat-cloth”) — a small cloth for the face, used to wipe the brow, to wrap a treasure, or to bind the head of the dead.

Biblical Definition

A napkin in the KJV is no table-linen but a small face-cloth — the sudarium, a hand’s breadth of fabric put to four uses in the New Testament, and every one of them instructive. It is the sloth’s hiding-place: the wicked servant returns his master’s money untraded, “Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin” (Luk 19:20) — the talent not squandered but wrapped, which is condemnation enough, for buried faithfulness is unfaithfulness. It is the badge of death: Lazarus came forth from the tomb bound hand and foot with graveclothes, “and his face was bound about with a napkin” (Joh 11:44), and had to be loosed, for he was raised only to die again. It is a channel of apostolic power: from Paul’s body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs and aprons (Act 19:12), the same word, in an age of signs now closed. But the napkin’s glory is in the empty tomb. Peter went in and saw the linen clothes lie, “and the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself” (Joh 20:7). It was not torn away, not tumbled, not carried off — it was folded and set apart, in the calm of One who had risen at leisure. Lazarus needed loosing; Christ left His grave-cloth behind Him in order, and the disciple that saw it believed.

Webster 1828 Definition

A small face-cloth (the Greek soudarion): used to wrap a treasure, to bind the head of the dead, and folded by itself in the empty tomb.

NAPKIN, a cloth for wiping the face; from the Old French nappe, “a cloth.”

It renders the Greek soudarion, from the Latin sudarium, a “sweat-cloth.”

In it the slothful servant hid his lord’s pound (Luk 19:20).

With it the face of the dead was bound about (Joh 11:44).

In the empty tomb it lay wrapped together in a place by itself (Joh 20:7).

Key Scripture

Luk 19:20 — "And another came, saying, Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin:"

Joh 11:44 — "And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go."

Joh 20:7 — "And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself."

Act 19:12 — "So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them."

Modern Corruption

The stolen-body theory, urged since Reimarus and the rationalists, is answered by a folded cloth: thieves do not tidy a grave.

expand to see more

The rationalist denial of the resurrection is as old as the guards at the sepulchre, who were paid to say, “His disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept” (Mat 28:13), and it was revived in the eighteenth century by Reimarus and the deists as the fraud hypothesis, which every generation of unbelief has since refurbished. The napkin answers it. A body snatched in haste by thieves in the dark is carried off wrapped, or the wrappings are torn away and flung down; what no robber does is unwind a hundred pound weight of spice-laden linen, leave it lying in its place, and then fold the face-cloth and set it apart by itself. The evidence in that tomb is not the evidence of theft; it is the evidence of a Man who rose from the dead without hurry and left the room in order. John looked at that folded cloth, and he believed.

The napkin also parts the two risings. Lazarus came out of his tomb still bound, his face bound about with a napkin, and had to be loosed by other men — a resuscitation, and a borrowed one; he wore his grave-clothes out of the grave because he would need them again. Christ left His behind. He passed out of the linen as He would pass through the doors, and the sweat-cloth of His dying lay folded where His head had been, a flag of a finished work. And the servant’s napkin at Luke 19 is the last warning: what is wrapped and laid up is not kept safe but lost. The Lord’s pound is given to be traded, and the man who folds his gift away in a cloth will find that the folding was the sin.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a small face-cloth — the Greek soudarion, a sweat-cloth.

expand to see more

Napkin — Old French nappe, “a cloth,” with the diminutive -kin.

It renders the Greek soudarion, from the Latin sudarium.

It denotes a small cloth for the face, not table-linen.

The slothful servant wrapped his lord’s pound in one (Luk 19:20).

In the empty tomb it lay folded in a place by itself (Joh 20:7).

Usage

"The pound kept laid up in a napkin was not kept safe but lost — buried faithfulness is unfaithfulness."

"Lazarus came forth bound, his face bound about with a napkin, and had to be loosed."

"The napkin lay folded by itself: thieves do not tidy a grave, and John believed."
